# **1. Introduction & Executive Summary** ###### **1.1 Introduction** The gold price so far this year has experienced a wide trading range. After an impressive rally at the end of 2010, gold suffered from a steep correction earlier this year, with the price falling by over $100 to a low of $1,319 in late January amidst both long liquidation and fresh short-side selling. Thereafter, however, it immediately rebounded and then rallied strongly to a fresh all-time-high of $1,541 in early May. Looking at the reasons behind the strength of gold prices over the last couple months, there is little doubt that the yellow metal benefited from escalating geopolitical tension in the Middle East and North Africa, which first emerged in February. These upheavals have impacted not only the gold market but also the wider commodity sector. With the oil price now trading in excess of $100/bbl, investors have become increasingly concerned by the potential longer-term inflationary risks. In fact, even before the recent surge in oil prices, inflationary pressures had already become heightened in some emerging markets and certainly in China, where it has contributed to robust levels of Chinese investment demand for gold bullion bars. Other factors that have encouraged investor buying have concerned growing public indebtedness in developed economies, coupled with continued and extremely low interest rates. For example, the average public debt ratio for advanced economies is forecast to surpass 100% of GDP in 2011. Such concerns have already triggered a further downgrading of the sovereign debt ratings of several developed economies, including Greece, Ireland, Japan, Portugal and Spain. Moreover, in April, Standard and Poor’s surprised the market with its announcement to place US sovereign credit on a negative outlook. Indeed, despite the lingering risks associated with sovereign debt in some European economies, the euro rose to a 16-month high against the dollar in late April this year, mainly due to the perceived lack of credibility concerning the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy in response to the inflation threat. Besides these factors, the gold price has also benefited from a number of positive developments relating to its underlying fundamentals. and the extended period for which interest rates are likely to be maintained at or near current levels.  In addition, given ample global liquidity and low interest rates prevailing in developed economies, investors’ search for higher yields is pushing them increasingly to broader commodity markets including gold.  Meanwhile, although central banks in the emerging markets have already started to tighten their monetary policies, real interest rates for savers are likely to remain firmly negative throughout this year, especially in China, which should encourage more demand for gold as a safe haven asset. 

Further aiding investment demand for gold will be persistent pressure in Europe’s credit markets, which could pose a material threat to the vulnerable and under capitalised European banking system.  As bond yields in Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Spain have continued to trade at record highs (at the time of this writing), the safe haven characteristic of gold will be highlighted, with further waves of investment in the yellow metal set to emerge.  In addition, we assume that the focus of this crisis will eventually move across the Atlantic and centre on the world’s largest debtor nation.  Indeed, unlike many European countries, the federal government not only lacks a “credible strategy” for dealing with its rampant debt, but it has continued to expand deficit spending at a time when it should be contracting.  In our view, this is likely to result

in renewed weakness in the dollar later this year. As such, under our **Base Case** (weighted with a 50% probability), we expect to see further gains in investment demand this year and for this to drive gold to register an impressive year-on-year increase (basis the annual average) of 22% to a fresh all-time high of $1,490 in 2011. Moving to 2012, we would assume the aforementioned factors will continue to support gold investment, with the price trading above $1,400 for much of the year. Given the reluctance of central banks to tighten monetary policy, particularly in the United States, we expect short-term interest rates to remain at low levels over much of the year. Thereafter, as the global economy returns to stable growth, with interest rates continuing to rise across developed countries, investment demand will eventually start to decline. In addition to the Base Case, we also offer two alternative scenarios for the global economy that are very different to our central forecast. In each instance, these have distinct implications for the level and trajectory of gold prices over the next three years. **Scenario B** (with a 30% probability) presents the most positive outlook for gold prices, with an investorled bull market continuing throughout the forecast period. Over this timeframe, investment is expected to be principally driven by concerns over a rapid rise in inflation rates, particularly in the United States where the CPI is forecast to rise to 5.5% by 2013. The main cause of this is the substantial level of liquidity that has been pumped into the market by the US Federal Reserve, with a distinct possibility that the Fed will engage in ‘QE3’. Furthermore, it is very likely that the authorities will be tempted to tolerate a rise in inflation if this boosts GDP growth and reduces the real level of public debt. In line with t

his, Scenario B also envisages a sharp drop in the value of the US dollar, which is forecast to fall to an annual average of $1.57 against the euro in 2013. A complete contrast is **Scenario C** (with a 20% probability), where investment in gold will start to decline this year.  Under this variant, after reaching a peak of $1,390 in 2011, the average annual price then declines, dropping to $1,230 and $1,070 in 2012 and 2013 respectively.  This is basis a secular recovery in the dollar and a low level of inflation, reflecting governments’ failure to boost private demand and consumer spending in advanced economies. 

The negative impact on gold investment of a prolonged period of low inflation in western countries will be compounded by tighter monetary policy and other administrative measures that will be undertaken in key emerging economies (such as China and India) to combat rising local inflation, which will also drag down the rate of world GDP growth.  These factors should also reduce gold’s appeal to investors, most notably in the final two forecast years, when a marked reduction in investment results in prices slipping to levels that are more in line with gold’s underlying supply/demand fundamentals.  It is of note that the gold price under this scenario has been revised upward noticeably compared with our previous forecast, reflecting the heightened investor interest in gold so far this year. 

Much of the above discussion has focused on the interplay between changes in the principal economic variables and investment demand.  As mentioned previously, however, we do not subscribe to the view that price direction and level are determined by investment alone.  The following analysis of expected trends in the underlying supply/demand variables shows that these will also play an important, even if subsidiary, role in gold price determination over the next three years.

###### **4.3 Developing World** 

Last year scrap flows emanating from the developing world, in apparent defiance of the 26% rise in average dollar gold prices, fell markedly from the unprecedented levels reached in 2009.  There were a number of factors that led to the declines in these supposedly price sensitive markets, which in some cases were acute (44% and 30% in Turkey and India, respectively, for example).  First, consumers in several markets had become acclimatised to the new, higher price level. Second, many held bullish longer term expectations and, in an environment of lower price volatility, there were fewer short-term opportunities to exploit and so many were often reluctant to liquidate gold assets. Third, weakness in the US dollar meant that in many cases the gold price in domestic currencies failed to register quite the same percentage gains as dollar prices.  Lastly, there was a degree of depletion in near market stocks in some markets, with jewellery holdings already having been liquidated, typicall

y during previous periods of high prices. 

A key characteristic of most of these markets is the dominance of low labour cost and high carat jewellery. This means that means gold jewellery is often viewed as quasi-investment vehicle, with consumers (most often women) willing to “invest” in plain jewellery with the clear intention of selling back should the gold price move in a favourable direction and a profit be obtained. As such, gold jewellery is often returned to the market during periods of elevated or volatile gold prices.  The adornment quality of the jewellery item and the use of precious and non-precious stones nonetheless still play an import role in the purchasing decision. 

In recent years there has been a notable change from what was viewed as typical jewellery styles which characterised many developing world markets, namely heavy, plain designs.  However, the rally in the gold price has meant fabricators have been forced to reduce the precious metal content, with lighter items and a greater use of stone set jewellery employed in order to attract a declining consumer base.  In addition, the younger generation has shown some preference for lower carat designs as a fashion item, rather than simply as an investment source, preferring something that can be worn for everyday use rather than for special occasions. ###### **7.1  Introduction** 

Following the heavy losses realised in 2009, world jewellery consumption partially recovered last year, as it rose by 11%. Elsewhere, demand was little changed in 2010, which suggests that the benefits of an improving global economy were broadly offset by firmer prices. 

Under the **Base Case** , we are expecting a slight rise in jewellery offtake this year, despite gold’s anticipated price increase.
